newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: No tribalist backing for S. African constitution.
newsitem.headline: No tribalist backing for S. African constitution.

text.p: South African constitutional negotiators on Thursday agreed final details of a draft blueprint for post-apartheid rule but failed to win support from a boycotting Zulu party.

"We have complied with all the requirements for certification of the constitution. What remains is the meeting of the Constitutional Assembly (CA) tomorrow...then we will be home and dry," CA chairman Cyril Ramaphosa said after a late-night meeting in the Cape Town parliament.
A 490-member CA is likely to give near unanimous support on Friday to the amended draft approved by negotiators.

The first draft was adopted by an overwhelming majority on May 8, but was referred back by the country's top court for further work on eight shortcomings ranging from an illegal labour relations clause to the inadequate entrenchment of a bill of right.

Senator Bulelani Ngcuka of the ruling African National Congress (ANC) said a government delegation met members of Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) on Thursday for renewed talks on their constitutional demands.
"We agreed that traditional leaders play a vital role in our society and that we need to create options to accommodate them," he said.
But the two sides could not agree on a role for unelected tribal leaders in democratic local governments.
"Unfortunately we will not be able to have the IFP rejoining discussions in the CA tomorrow," he said.

Inkatha ended an 18-month boycott of the Constitutional Assembly for a week earlier this month, but quit again when their demand for recognition of tribal leaders as the primary local authority in traditional areas was rejected.

In an unexpected concession to Inkatha, however, delegates agreed in the absence of any member of the traditionalist party to extend the existing right of traditional leaders to seats in municipal governments until the next local polls in 1999.

"This clause should be taken as a reflection of the seriousness with which the ANC has been willing to engage the IFP, listen to them and try to reach some accommodation that would go some way to addressing some of the concerns of the IFP," said ANC negotiator Blade Nzimande.
He said the concession effectively granted Inkatha a further two years to negotiate a role for the tribal leaders who dominate conservative Zulu society.
Without the concession, tribal leaders would have been ousted as soon as the new constitution is implemented some time in the first half of 1997.

Zulu analysts from the Inkatha stronghold province of KwaZulu-Natal said privately they feared a dramatic escalation of the 10-year-old conflict in the region if tribal leaders were forced to accept the authority of elected councillors.
